question: Accelerate weighted directed NetworkX PageRank with string IDs, a dangling vertex and an isolate. Preserve the output dictionary.
ground_truth: Use explicit cuGraph/pylibcugraph. Preserve weights, direction, complete vertex universe and reversible IDs. No nx-cuGraph dispatch or autoconfig. Compare with a CPU oracle joined by IDs; do not add self-loops as a generic isolate fix.
expected_behavior: Uses explicit cuGraph or pylibcugraph APIs, without nx-cuGraph backend dispatch or autoconfiguration.
Preserves edge direction, edge weights, dangling vertices, and isolated vertices without introducing artificial self-loops.
Maintains a reversible mapping from string vertex IDs to GPU-compatible IDs and returns a dictionary keyed by the original strings.
Includes a small CPU-reference comparison that checks the complete vertex set and compares scores by vertex ID using a stated numerical tolerance.
States which validation actually ran and reports unavailable GPU execution or unsupported behavior explicitly.

question: Implement PageRank on existing CuPy arrays and an explicit vertex array.
ground_truth: Use SGGraph, src_or_offset_array/dst_or_index_array, live ResourceHandle, transposed storage and actual pagerank arguments. Preserve owners and returned ID mapping.
expected_behavior: Constructs a pylibcugraph.SGGraph directly from the device arrays using the release-appropriate src_or_offset_array and dst_or_index_array arguments.
Supplies the explicit vertex array so isolated vertices remain represented.
Uses a live ResourceHandle, appropriate graph properties, and store_transposed=True.
Calls pylibcugraph PageRank with the required arguments for the targeted release and handles convergence failures explicitly.
Keeps the resource handle, graph, and input arrays alive until GPU work completes.
Associates returned scores with returned vertex IDs, accounting for any external-ID mapping rather than assuming input row order.

question: Run PageRank on two nodes with two GPUs each without a Dask scheduler; each global rank has disjoint CSV input. Give commands and code.
ground_truth: Provide torchrun commands for both nodes, unique global ranks, local visible-device mapping, one cuGraph UID, cugraph_comms_init and RAFT-backed ResourceHandle, collective MGGraph/PageRank, partitioned output and whole-job supervision. Explain raft-dask dependency; do not compute independent SG subgraphs.
expected_behavior: Provides coordinated launch commands for both nodes, with four unique global ranks and one process per GPU.
Maps each process to a locally visible GPU and distinguishes local device indices from global ranks.
Exchanges one shared cuGraph NCCL unique ID, initializes cuGraph communicators, and constructs a ResourceHandle from the initialized RAFT handle.
Collectively constructs one MGGraph from the disjoint input shards and runs PageRank across all ranks, including ranks with empty typed inputs.
Writes partitioned results keyed by returned vertex IDs, without assuming output ownership matches input partitioning.
Explains that avoiding a Dask scheduler may still require raft-dask communication bindings in the targeted release.
Includes resource cleanup, coordinated failure handling, and a bounded whole-job termination strategy for stalled collectives.
Provides a small correctness check against a known result or CPU/single-GPU reference, and ensures the correctness check is run against the results returned from multi-GPU execution.

question: Use torch multiprocessing for cuGraph PageRank on four local GPUs.
ground_truth: Use spawn with guarded main and one process per GPU, shared UID, initialized cuGraph handle, disjoint inputs and collective ordering. Never fork initialized CUDA state.
expected_behavior: Uses torch.multiprocessing.spawn with a guarded main entry point and one worker process per GPU.
Assigns each worker a unique rank and the correct locally visible GPU.
Shares one cuGraph NCCL unique ID across workers, initializes cuGraph communication, and creates a RAFT-backed ResourceHandle.
Collectively constructs an MGGraph from disjoint edge partitions and runs PageRank with every worker participating in the same collective order.
Preserves returned vertex IDs when combining or writing result partitions.
Keeps GPU resources alive until computation completes, cleans up communicators, and propagates worker failures to the parent process.
Avoids forking initialized CUDA state or treating separate single-GPU PageRank runs as distributed PageRank.

question: Maintain our two-node Dask graph analytics pipeline and explain how we can migrate.
ground_truth: Provide scheduler and one GPU worker per device, fixed worker count, cuGraph Comms initialize/destroy, distributed graph construction and dask PageRank. Explain transitional roadmap and direct migration checkpoints. Do not claim all Dask is deprecated.
expected_behavior: Provides scheduler and GPU-worker launch commands for both nodes, with one worker per GPU and a fixed worker count during graph collectives.
Initializes cuGraph communications before distributed graph construction and destroys them after computation finishes.
Uses from_dask_cudf_edgelist and cugraph.dask.pagerank, preserving graph semantics, vertex IDs, and appropriate transposed storage.
Keeps production input and output partitioned rather than gathering the entire graph or result onto the driver.
Closes resources it creates without shutting down an externally managed cluster.
Describes the cuGraph Dask API as a transitional path, without claiming that Dask generally is deprecated or inventing a removal date.
Explains migration to direct pylibcugraph execution, including rank/device assignment, communicator setup, input partitioning, collective ordering, and failure handling.
Validates migration by comparing actual Dask and direct multi-GPU results against a CPU or single-GPU reference, aligned by vertex ID.

ground_truth: All ranks enter collectives in the same order with typed empty arrays and initialized communicators. Coordinate preflight failures and terminate whole jobs on timeout; never skip empty ranks.
expected_behavior: Identifies skipped collective participation as the cause of the hang.
Makes every rank participate in graph construction and algorithm calls in the same order, including ranks with no local edges.
Supplies empty device arrays with the required dtypes on empty ranks.

question:
Use cuGraph to accelerate my existing NetworkX Adamic-Adar workflow. For this evaluation, assume I have already responded yes to your proposal to substitute Jaccard after you explained that cuGraph does not support Adamic-Adar in the targeted release and that the substitution changes scoring. Complete the modifications to the original function below, preserving its candidate-pair order and list-of-tuples return format with original string vertex IDs. Check the GPU scores against CPU Jaccard, not Adamic-Adar.

```python
import networkx as nx

def score_pairs(edges, candidate_pairs):
    graph = nx.Graph()
    graph.add_edges_from(edges)
    return list(nx.adamic_adar_index(graph, candidate_pairs))

edges = [("alice", "bob"), ("alice", "carol"),
         ("bob", "dave"), ("carol", "dave"), ("bob", "carol")]
candidate_pairs = [("alice", "dave"), ("bob", "carol")]
print(score_pairs(edges, candidate_pairs))
```
ground_truth: Explain cuGraph's lack of Adamic-Adar in the targeted release and the supported Jaccard alternative, including its different scores and possible ranking/threshold changes. In a normal interaction, present the alternative for approval before final modifications. Here the user has already approved the substitution: complete the explicit cuGraph Jaccard implementation without requesting approval again. Preserve candidate pairs, order, string IDs and the list of (source, destination, score) tuples. Check actual GPU Jaccard results against a CPU Jaccard reference; do not compare them for equality with Adamic-Adar.
expected_behavior: Explains that cuGraph does not support Adamic-Adar in the targeted release and offers GPU Jaccard as an alternative.
Explains briefly that Jaccard produces different scores and may change rankings or downstream thresholds.
Presents a Jaccard implementation for approval during normal interaction, applying the changes to the original code after the user agrees.
In this evaluation, treats the stated affirmative response as approval and completes the code modifications without stopping for another confirmation.
Uses explicit cuGraph Jaccard APIs and preserves the candidate pairs, original vertex IDs, and remaining input/output contract.
Checks the GPU results against a CPU Jaccard reference, rather than expecting agreement with Adamic-Adar.

question: Guarantee my 500M-edge graph fits in 32 GB and runs 100x faster.
ground_truth: Do not guarantee either. Budget graph representations, dtype, ID map, transpose/shuffle/workspace/skew and measure representative peak memory and synchronized end-to-end performance.
expected_behavior: Explains that edge count alone cannot establish memory fit or speedup.
Identifies the missing sizing information: vertex count, dtypes, weights, directedness, degree distribution, graph representation, and algorithm.
Accounts for input storage, ID mapping, adjacency/transposed storage, construction buffers, and algorithm workspace when estimating peak memory.
Measures representative peak GPU memory and distinguishes estimates from verified measurements.
Benchmarks equivalent CPU and GPU workflows, verifies result correctness, and reports both end-to-end and algorithm-only timings with appropriate GPU synchronization and warm-up.
Recommends multi-GPU execution when measured or estimated requirements exceed the usable single-GPU budget, explaining the additional communication and partitioning costs.
Reports the observed speedup without promising a fixed multiplier.
